title: The Tree Rings That Dated a Tsunami

p: A

Along the coast of Washington State there are groves of dead red cedar standing in salt marsh. The trees are grey and bare, and they have been called ghost forests for as long as anyone has written about them.
B

Cedar does not grow in salt water. For the trees to have died standing, the ground they grew on must have dropped suddenly, far enough and fast enough to let the tide reach their roots before they could be washed away.
C

Oral histories kept by the Makah, the Quileute and other peoples of the coast describe a night when the ground shook and the sea came in. The accounts place the event several generations before the first European ships arrived.
D
A tree keeps a ring for every year it grows. The outermost ring of the ghost cedars is complete, with the dense latewood that forms at the end of a growing season, and no ring begins after it.
E

That narrows the death of the trees to the months between the end of one growing season and the start of the next, which in that climate means somewhere between the autumn of 1699 and the spring of 1700.
F

Eight thousand kilometres away, Japanese officials recorded a wave that flooded villages on the Pacific coast on the night of January 27, 1700. No earthquake had been felt in Japan, so the records call it an orphan tsunami.
G

Each piece on its own proves little. A ghost forest could have many causes, and an unexplained wave could have come from anywhere. Together the three lines of evidence fix an earthquake off the coast of North America to a single night.

What does the complete outer ring on the ghost cedars tell investigators?
It has the dense latewood that forms at the end of a growing season and no ring begins after it, so the trees died between the autumn of 1699 and the spring of 1700.
paragraph focus
Paragraph C (i.e. the oral histories of the coastal peoples) and paragraph F (i.e. the Japanese record of the orphan tsunami).
summarize
Summarize how three kinds of evidence were used to date one earthquake.

Dead cedar standing in salt marsh shows the coast dropped suddenly. Oral histories of the Makah and Quileute describe a night of shaking and flooding. Tree rings put the death of the trees between autumn 1699 and spring 1700, and Japanese officials recorded an orphan tsunami on January 27, 1700.
vocabulary

orphan tsunami: a wave recorded with no earthquake felt nearby, so its source is unknown at the time.
latewood: the dense wood a tree lays down at the end of a growing season.
connection
Describe the connection between the fact that cedar does not grow in salt water and the conclusion that the ground dropped.
For the trees to have died standing in salt marsh, the ground they grew on must have dropped suddenly, far enough and fast enough to let the tide reach their roots.
note: RI.7.1 asks for several pieces of evidence, so the answer worth pushing for names all three, i.e. the ghost forest, the oral histories and the Japanese record. One of the three is not yet an argument.

title: The Orphan Trains

p: A

Between 1854 and 1929 the Children's Aid Society and other organizations put roughly two hundred thousand children on trains out of New York and sent them west to live with families they had never met.
B

The man who began the programme, Charles Loring Brace, argued that a child raised on a farm would do better than one raised in a city institution. The city was full of children sleeping in doorways, and the almshouses were worse.
C
A train would stop at a town, and the children would be lined up on a platform or a stage in a hall. Local families looked them over, asked questions, and sometimes felt their arms for strength.
D

Some children were adopted outright and remembered the day as the best of their lives. Others were taken as unpaid farm labour, and agents who were meant to check on them a year later often never came.
E

The Society kept records, and those records are one-sided. They were written by the people running the programme, who had every reason to count a placement as a success unless something had plainly gone wrong.
F

Letters written by the children themselves survive in smaller numbers. They describe being separated from brothers and sisters on the same platform, and some of them spent decades afterwards trying to find each other.
G
Both kinds of document are evidence. A history that uses only the Society's files describes a rescue, and one that uses only the letters describes a loss, and the programme was in fact both at once.

Why does the article say the Society's records are one-sided?

Paragraph E (i.e. the Society's own records) and paragraph F (i.e. the letters written by the children).

Summarize what the orphan trains were and why they are hard to judge.

Between 1854 and 1929 about two hundred thousand children were sent west by train to families they had never met. Some were adopted and some were taken as unpaid farm labour. The Society's records count placements as successes and the children's letters describe families separated, so each kind of evidence tells a different story.
vocabulary

almshouse: a public institution where people with no money were housed.
placement: the act of putting a child with a family, which is also the word the Society used when counting its results.
connection
Describe the connection between who wrote a document and what that document shows.
The Society's files were written by the people running the programme and describe a rescue, while the letters were written by the children and describe being separated from brothers and sisters.
note: A good answer cites at least two documents with different authors, i.e. the Society's records and the children's letters. Noticing who wrote a source is the move RI.7.1 is building toward.

title: The Bird That Builds a Compost Heap

p: A
Most birds sit on their eggs. The malleefowl of southern Australia does not, and the alternative it has worked out takes the better part of a year to run.
B

In autumn the male scrapes a pit several metres across and fills it with leaves and twigs. Rain soaks the pile, and the material begins to rot, which releases heat exactly the way a garden compost heap does.
C

When the pile is warm enough the bird covers it with sand, and the female lays her eggs inside. An egg sits in the mound for seven or eight weeks, and nothing about the arrangement is adjustable from outside.
D
The temperature has to stay close to thirty-three degrees. Too cool and the eggs do not develop; too warm and they die. The rotting leaves do not hold a steady temperature on their own.
E
So the male tests the mound. He pushes his beak into the sand, and the sensitivity of his bill and mouth tells him whether the inside is warm or cool, and then he adds sand or digs it away.
F
Later in the season the rotting slows and the sun takes over as the main source of heat. The bird's work changes with it: he opens the mound in the morning and closes it before the afternoon.
G
A chick digs its own way out, which can take fifteen hours, and then runs. Its parents do not feed it, do not recognise it, and may be standing a few metres away while it leaves.

How does the male malleefowl know whether to add sand or dig it away?
He pushes his beak into the sand, and the sensitivity of his bill and mouth tells him whether the inside of the mound is warm or cool.
paragraph focus
Paragraph D (i.e. why the temperature matters) and paragraph E (i.e. how the bird tests and corrects it).
summarize
Summarize how a malleefowl incubates its eggs without sitting on them.

The male fills a pit with leaves and twigs that rot and give off heat, then covers it with sand for the female to lay in. He tests the mound with his beak and adds or removes sand to hold it near thirty-three degrees, and later he opens and closes it as the sun takes over from the rotting.
vocabulary

incubate: to keep eggs at the temperature they need in order to develop.
mound: here, the pile of rotting material and sand the bird builds and manages, not a natural hill.
connection
Describe the connection between the rotting slowing down and the change in the bird's daily work.
Once the rotting slows the sun becomes the main source of heat, so the bird opens the mound in the morning and closes it before the afternoon instead of only adding or removing sand.
note: Three separate pieces of evidence show the mound is managed rather than just built, i.e. the beak test, the adding and removing of sand, and the switch to opening and closing. Push for more than one.

title: The Blizzard That Buried the Wires

p: A

In March 1888 a storm stalled over the north-east of the United States and snowed for three days. Drifts in New York City reached the second floor of some buildings, and about four hundred people died.
B

The city above the streets was a tangle of wire. Telegraph, telephone, fire alarm and electric light companies had each strung their own lines, and in places the poles carried so many that they blocked the light.
C

Wet snow freezes onto a wire and builds a sleeve of ice around it. The weight of that sleeve, multiplied across a span, is far more than the wire was built to hold, and the poles came down across the streets.
D

With the wires down, the city could not send a fire alarm, could not call a doctor, and could not reach the trains that were stopped outside it. Food deliveries stopped for days in some neighbourhoods.
E

Arguments for putting the lines underground had been made for years before the storm. They had lost, mainly because burying a line cost far more than hanging one and because the companies owning the poles saw no reason to pay.
F
The storm did not introduce a new argument. What it changed was the price of ignoring the old one, and within a few years New York had begun moving its wires into conduits beneath the pavement.
G

Boston and other cities followed. The ice storm is sometimes described as the cause, which is not quite right: the engineering case was already made, and the storm settled who was going to pay for it.

Why did the overhead wires fail during the storm?
Wet snow freezes onto a wire and builds a sleeve of ice, and the weight of that sleeve across a span is far more than the wire was built to hold, so the poles came down.
paragraph focus
Paragraph E (i.e. why burying the lines had lost the argument before) and paragraph F (i.e. what the storm actually changed).
summarize
Summarize what the 1888 blizzard did to New York's wires and what followed.

Three days of snow brought down the overhead telegraph, telephone, fire alarm and light wires, so the city could not send an alarm or call a doctor. Burying the lines had been argued for years and had lost on cost, and after the storm New York began moving its wires into conduits beneath the pavement.
vocabulary

conduit: a pipe or channel laid underground to carry wires.
stalled: here, a storm that stopped moving and stayed over one area instead of passing through.
connection
Describe the connection between the cost of burying a line and the delay in doing it.
Burying a line cost far more than hanging one and the companies owning the poles saw no reason to pay, so the argument for underground wires lost for years before the storm.
note: The last paragraph is the one to slow down on. The text explicitly refuses the simple cause, i.e. "the engineering case was already made, and the storm settled who was going to pay for it."

title: The Lead in the Greenland Ice

p: A
Snow that falls on the Greenland ice sheet does not melt. It is buried by the next year's snow, compressed into ice, and stays where it is, in order, for thousands of years.
B
A drilled core brings that order up as a column. Summer and winter snow differ in texture, so the layers can be counted the way tree rings are counted, and a depth can be converted into a date.
C

The ice also traps whatever was in the air. Dust from a desert, ash from an eruption and the chemistry of the atmosphere itself are all held in place, which makes the core a record and not just a measurement.
D

In cores covering the last three thousand years, the lead content rises sharply, holds high for several centuries, and then collapses. The rise begins around 600 BCE and the collapse falls in the third century CE.
E

Lead does not blow off a mountain by itself in those quantities. Smelting silver releases it, and silver smelting on a large scale is exactly what the Greek and then the Roman economies did to make coins.
F

The collapse is the harder part of the claim and the more interesting one. It lines up with a period of plague and political crisis in the Roman world, when mining output is known from other sources to have fallen.
G
The ice does not say Rome. It says lead, at a depth that corresponds to a date. Everything after that is an argument built by putting the ice beside coins, mine workings and written records.

How can a depth in an ice core be turned into a date?
Summer and winter snow differ in texture, so the layers can be counted the way tree rings are counted and a depth converted into a date.
paragraph focus
Paragraph D (i.e. what the lead measurements show) and paragraph G (i.e. what the ice does and does not say on its own).
summarize
Summarize what the lead in Greenland ice shows and how far the evidence reaches.

Snow buried on the ice sheet keeps a layered record that traps what was in the air, so the layers can be counted and dated. Lead rises around 600 BCE, holds high, and collapses in the third century CE, which matches large-scale silver smelting and then a crisis in the Roman world, but the ice only shows lead at a depth and the rest is argued from coins and written records.
vocabulary

core: a column of ice drilled out whole so its layers stay in the order they formed.
smelting: heating ore to separate out a metal, which in the case of silver also releases lead.
connection
Describe the connection between smelting silver and the lead measured in the ice.
Smelting silver releases lead, and Greek and Roman economies smelted silver on a large scale to make coins, which is why lead does not blow off a mountain by itself in those quantities.
note: The last paragraph draws the line between measurement and argument, i.e. "the ice does not say Rome." A student who cites only the lead curve has half the case.

title: The Canal and the Mosquito

p: A
The French began digging a canal across Panama in 1881 and gave up eight years later. The engineering had defeated them, and so had a death rate that reached into the thousands.
B

Yellow fever and malaria killed workers faster than the company could replace them. Hospitals of the period set the legs of beds in pans of water to keep ants off the patients, which bred mosquitoes beside every sickbed.
C

By the time the United States took the project over in 1904, Carlos Finlay and Walter Reed had shown that yellow fever is carried by a mosquito. William Gorgas was given the job of acting on that finding.
D

His campaign was not medical in the ordinary sense. Crews drained standing water, oiled ponds, screened buildings and fumigated houses across the whole zone, and yellow fever disappeared from the isthmus within two years.
E
The engineering changed too. Rather than cutting a channel at sea level, the American plan dammed the Chagres River to make a lake and lifted ships over the high ground in locks.
F
Neither decision would have worked alone. A workforce that is dying cannot build a lock system, and a lock system that does not exist cannot be saved by healthy workers.
G
The canal opened in 1914. It is usually told as a story about concrete and excavation, and the second half of the story is a mosquito that had to be removed from the ground the concrete stood on.

Why did hospitals of the period make the mosquito problem worse?
They set the legs of beds in pans of water to keep ants off the patients, which bred mosquitoes beside every sickbed.
paragraph focus
Paragraph D (i.e. the campaign against the mosquito) and paragraph E (i.e. the change to a lock and lake design).
summarize
Summarize the two changes that let the canal be finished.

The French gave up in 1889 after yellow fever and malaria killed thousands of workers. After 1904 William Gorgas drained and oiled standing water, screened buildings and fumigated houses until yellow fever disappeared, and the American plan dammed the Chagres River to lift ships in locks instead of cutting at sea level. Neither change would have worked without the other.
vocabulary

isthmus: a narrow strip of land joining two larger landmasses, which is what Panama is.
fumigate: to fill a space with smoke or chemical vapour in order to kill insects.
connection
Describe the connection between the health campaign and the engineering plan.
A workforce that is dying cannot build a lock system, and a lock system that does not exist cannot be saved by healthy workers, so neither decision would have worked alone.
note: RI.7.2 wants two central ideas held at once. A summary that covers only the mosquitoes or only the locks has found one idea and stopped.

title: The Factory Whistle

p: A
Before factories, most work was measured by the task. A weaver finished a length of cloth, a farmer brought in a field, and how long either took was a private matter between the worker and the work.
B
A mill cannot run that way. Water wheels and then steam engines drove every machine in a building from one shaft, so the whole floor had to start together and stop together or the power was wasted.
C

The whistle enforced that. Workers were paid for hours rather than output, which meant that for the first time an employer had a direct financial interest in exactly where a worker was at seven in the morning.
D
Clocks became common in ordinary houses in the same decades, and so did arguments about them. Mill owners were accused of running the factory clock slow at the start of a shift and fast at the end.
E

The second idea grew out of the first. Once time was the unit being bought, time became the thing to bargain over, and the ten-hour day and then the eight-hour day were demands that could not have been phrased earlier.
F

The slogan of the eight-hour movement divided a day into three: eight hours of work, eight of rest, and eight for what we will. It is an argument about time that only makes sense once time is being counted.
G
The whistle is therefore not only a signal. It marks the point at which the working day stopped being a description of what got done and became a quantity that two sides could argue about.

Why did a mill have to start and stop all its machines together?

title: What Lives in a Gut

p: A
A human intestine holds a large population of bacteria. Counting them is harder than it sounds, and older textbook figures were estimates built on estimates, but the number is in the trillions.
B
Most of these organisms cannot be grown in a dish. For a century that put them beyond study, because the standard method in microbiology was to isolate something and raise it on its own.
C
Sequencing changed the question. Instead of growing an organism, a laboratory can read genetic material straight out of a sample and work out what was there from the sequences it finds.
D
That produced a catalogue, and a catalogue invited a second question, which is harder: does the mixture do anything, or is it simply present the way dust is present in a house?
E

Some of the evidence is strong. Gut bacteria break down fibres that human enzymes cannot, and they make certain vitamins, and a person whose gut flora is wiped out by antibiotics is more easily infected by other organisms.
F

Other claims run ahead of their evidence. Studies linking gut bacteria to mood or behaviour are mostly in mice, often with small numbers, and a correlation in a mouse colony is not a mechanism in a person.
G
Both things are true at once, and a careful article says so. The catalogue is real and growing; the question of what the catalogue causes is open and is being answered slowly.

title: The Typewriter and the Office Door

p: A

The first commercially successful typewriter went on sale in 1874. It was slow to catch on, partly because a typed letter struck some recipients as rude, as though the writer had not troubled to use a pen.
B

What changed was the volume of paper. Railways, insurance firms and mail-order companies generated records faster than clerks could copy them, and a machine that produced legible text at speed solved a problem those firms actually had.
C
An office before the typewriter was almost entirely male. Clerking was a career with a ladder, and a young man who began copying letters could expect to be given responsibility over time.
D
The typewriter was new, so no one held it. Firms hiring typists could pay less by hiring women, and within thirty years the great majority of typists in the United States were women.
E
That gave many women their first access to paid work outside a factory or a home, and the training schools and the wages were real. It also built a job with a ceiling on it.
F
Typing was defined from the start as a separate track rather than the first rung of the clerical ladder. The men kept the ladder, and the new entrants were given a room with a door on it.
G
Both halves of that are the history. A machine opened an occupation to a group that had been shut out of it, and the same machine fixed the shape of the occupation they were let into.

Typing was a separate track from the start. It was not the first rung of the clerical ladder. The men kept the ladder. The new workers got a room with a door.
G
Both halves are the history. A machine opened a job to people shut out of it. The same machine fixed the shape of that job.

Why did firms begin to want typewriters?
Railways, insurance firms and mail-order companies generated records faster than clerks could copy them, and a machine that produced legible text at speed solved a problem those firms actually had.
paragraph focus
Paragraph E (i.e. the access the job gave) and paragraph F (i.e. the ceiling built into it).
summarize
Summarize the two things the typewriter did to office work.

Firms adopted the typewriter because they were producing records faster than clerks could copy them. Because the machine was new and nobody held it, firms hired women at lower pay, which gave many women their first paid work outside a factory or a home, and also fixed typing as a separate track from the clerical ladder.
vocabulary

clerical: to do with office work such as copying, filing and correspondence.
ceiling: here, a limit on how far a worker can be promoted, not part of a room.
connection
Describe the connection between the typewriter being a new machine and who was hired to use it.
Because the typewriter was new, no one held it, so firms hiring typists could pay less by hiring women and within thirty years most typists in the United States were women.
note: The gain and the limit are one story, not a good half and a bad half. A summary that reports only the opportunity has dropped an idea the text develops.

title: The Ring of Coral

p: A

A coral atoll is a ring of low islands around a lagoon, often far out in deep ocean. The shape is strange enough to need explaining: a ring of shallow-water animals with thousands of metres of water just outside it.
B

Reef-building corals need sunlight, because the algae living in their tissue supply much of their food. That confines them to roughly the top forty metres, which makes a reef in the deep ocean a contradiction.
C

Charles Darwin proposed an answer in 1842 after seeing atolls on the Beagle voyage. A volcano builds an island, coral grows as a fringe around its shore, and the volcano then subsides slowly beneath the sea.
D
If the coral grows upward at about the rate the island sinks, the reef stays in the sunlight while the land inside it disappears. What is left is a ring with a lagoon where the mountain used to be.
E

The second idea is about how such a claim gets settled. Darwin's account predicted something specific: beneath an atoll there should be a great thickness of shallow-water coral sitting on volcanic rock.
F

Nobody could test that for a century. Drilling at Enewetak Atoll in 1952 went down more than a kilometre through coral limestone and struck basalt, which is what the prediction required and what a rival explanation did not.
G
So the atoll is two stories. One is how a ring of islands forms, and the other is how an idea proposed from the deck of a ship waited a hundred years for a drill.

Why can reef-building corals only live near the surface?

Paragraph D (i.e. how the ring is left behind) and paragraph F (i.e. the drilling at Enewetak).
summarize
Summarize Darwin's explanation of atolls and how it was tested.

vocabulary

connection
Describe the connection between the rate the coral grows and the rate the island sinks.

title: The Chemist Who Fed and Poisoned

p: A

Plants need nitrogen, and the air is nearly four fifths nitrogen, but the atmospheric form is locked in a bond so stable that almost nothing alive can break it. Farming therefore depended on manure, on clover, and on mined deposits that were running down.
B

In 1909 Fritz Haber combined nitrogen and hydrogen under great pressure and heat over a catalyst and produced ammonia. Carl Bosch turned the laboratory result into an industrial process, and by 1913 a factory was making fertilizer out of air.
C

It is difficult to overstate what followed. A large share of the nitrogen in the body of a person alive today passed through that reaction, and the population the earth now supports is not reachable by the older methods.
D
The same chemistry has another use. Explosives need fixed nitrogen too, and when war came in 1914 the process that was feeding Germany was also supplying the material its artillery fired.
E

Haber went further than supplying it. He argued for chemical weapons, developed the method, and stood on the field at Ypres in April 1915 when chlorine was released from cylinders toward the French line.
F
His wife Clara Immerwahr was a chemist too, the first woman to take a doctorate in chemistry at her university. She opposed the work, and days after Ypres she shot herself in their garden.
G

Haber received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for the ammonia synthesis. He left Germany in 1933 when the new government's laws reached him, and he died the following year. No summary of him holds still.

title: The Seed Collection Under Siege

p: A

Nikolai Vavilov spent the 1920s and 1930s collecting seed. He travelled across five continents gathering varieties of wheat, rice, maize and potato, and by 1940 his institute in Leningrad held the largest such collection in the world.
B

His reasoning was that a crop grown everywhere from one or two varieties is fragile. The wild and local relatives of that crop carry resistance to diseases that have not arrived yet, and once those varieties are gone they cannot be recovered.
C
The argument made him enemies. Trofim Lysenko rejected the genetics the collection was built on and had the backing of the state, and Vavilov was arrested in 1940 and died in prison in 1943.
D
German forces encircled Leningrad in September 1941. The siege lasted nearly nine hundred days, and starvation in the city killed hundreds of thousands of people during the first winter alone.
E

The institute held tonnes of rice, maize, wheat and several thousand varieties of potato, in a building in the middle of a starving city. The staff moved the collection into a basement and took turns guarding it.
F
Several of them died of starvation at their posts. Alexander Stchukin was found at his desk with a packet of groundnuts; Dmitri Ivanov died surrounded by sacks of rice he had not opened.
G
They were not protecting food. They were protecting the ability to grow food later, which is an abstraction, and the collection they kept has supplied breeding programmes ever since.

Describe the connection between an idea about plant disease and the decision those staff made.

title: The Bridge That Shook Itself Apart

p: A

The Tacoma Narrows Bridge opened in July 1940 and fell into the water four months later. Film of the collapse shows the deck twisting through an angle that looks impossible for a road to survive even briefly.
B

The bridge was slender by design. Its engineer, Leon Moisseiff, had argued that a deck could be made lighter and shallower than previous practice allowed, and the theory he used had been applied successfully on other spans.
C

It also moved from the day it opened. Drivers reported the deck rising and falling, local people called it Galloping Gertie, and the motion was treated as a nuisance to be damped rather than a warning.
D

The usual classroom explanation is resonance: wind gusts arriving at the frequency the bridge liked to vibrate at, pushing it like a child on a swing. That explanation is in a great many textbooks and it is wrong.
E

What happened is aeroelastic flutter. The deck's own twisting changed the way air flowed around it, that altered flow pushed the deck further in the direction it was already going, and the motion fed itself from a steady wind.
F

The difference matters because the two have different cures. Resonance is avoided by changing a frequency. Flutter is avoided by changing the shape of the deck so that twisting does not generate a force that deepens the twist.
G

Bridges built afterwards use open trusses or slotted decks that let air through. The lesson was not that the engineers miscalculated an old problem; it was that they had met a new one and named it wrongly for years.

What is aeroelastic flutter, as the article describes it?
The deck's own twisting changed the way air flowed around it, and that altered flow pushed the deck further in the direction it was already going, so the motion fed itself from a steady wind.

Paragraph D (i.e. the resonance explanation) and paragraph F (i.e. why the difference between the two changes the cure).

Summarize what brought the Tacoma Narrows Bridge down and why the common explanation is wrong.

vocabulary

resonance: pushing something at the frequency it already vibrates at, so the motion grows.
truss: an open framework of beams, used here instead of a solid deck so that air can pass through.
connection
Describe the connection between naming the cause correctly and designing later bridges.

title: The Nurse Who Drew a Diagram

p: A

Florence Nightingale arrived at the British military hospital at Scutari in 1854, during the war in the Crimea. Soldiers were dying there in numbers that nobody in London had expected or could explain.
B

She began counting. The hospital kept records so poorly that even the number of deaths was uncertain, and her first work was not nursing but building a system that produced a trustworthy figure every month.
C

What the figures showed was that most of the dead had not been killed by their wounds. They were dying of typhus, cholera and dysentery, contracted in the hospital, in a building standing over a blocked sewer.
D

Reporting a table of monthly deaths to a government committee is a way of being ignored. Nightingale drew the numbers instead, as wedges radiating from a centre, with the area of each wedge standing for the deaths in a month.
E

The diagram splits each wedge by cause, and the part representing preventable disease dwarfs the part representing wounds. A reader does not have to follow an argument to see it; the picture makes the comparison before the text does.
F

The sanitary commission dug out the sewers and improved ventilation, and the death rate fell. Attributing that fall entirely to the diagram would be too neat, because several changes happened together.
G

What is not in doubt is the method. Nightingale was elected the first woman fellow of the Royal Statistical Society in 1858, and the argument she made was carried by a drawing that an official could not put aside.

What did Nightingale's figures show about how the soldiers were dying?
Most of the dead had not been killed by their wounds but were dying of typhus, cholera and dysentery contracted in the hospital, which stood over a blocked sewer.

Paragraph D (i.e. why she drew the numbers) and paragraph F (i.e. the caution about what caused the death rate to fall).

Summarize what Nightingale counted and why she drew it.

preventable: able to be stopped by action taken beforehand, which is what the diagram showed most of the deaths were.
sanitary: to do with cleanliness and drainage, especially the removal of sewage.

Describe the connection between the form of her diagram and the effect it had on officials.
The area of each wedge stood for the deaths in a month and each wedge was split by cause, so a reader could see that preventable disease dwarfed wounds without having to follow an argument.

title: The Eruption That Cancelled a Summer

p: A
Mount Tambora, on the island of Sumbawa, erupted in April 1815. It was the largest eruption anywhere in recorded history, and it removed roughly a third of the height of the mountain.
B
The local destruction was immediate. Ash buried villages, and the kingdoms on the slopes ceased to exist. What happened afterwards was slower and reached places that had never heard of the mountain.
C

An eruption of that size pushes sulphur dioxide into the stratosphere, above the weather. There it forms tiny droplets of sulphuric acid that scatter sunlight back into space and stay aloft for a year or more.
D

The following year, 1816, is remembered in New England and in Europe as the year without a summer. Snow fell in June in Massachusetts, frost killed crops through the growing season, and harvests failed across much of Europe.
E

The consequences were social. Food prices rose, people in Switzerland and elsewhere went hungry, and the failed harvests pushed families off farms in Vermont and New Hampshire and westward into Ohio and Indiana.
F

Nobody at the time connected any of it to a mountain in the Dutch East Indies. The link was argued much later, from ice cores holding the sulphate layer, from tree rings recording a cold year, and from ships' logs and parish records.
G
That is the shape of the story: an event, then a mechanism nobody could see, then consequences on another continent, and only afterwards a chain of evidence joining them together.

title: What a Scientist Means by Significant

p: A
In ordinary speech, significant means important. A significant change in the weather is one you would notice, and a significant amount of money is an amount worth having.
B

In a research paper the word is doing a different job. It describes how likely a result is to have come up by chance alone, and it says nothing at all about whether the result is large or whether it matters.
C

The usual test asks a narrow question. Suppose the treatment does nothing: how often would an experiment like this one produce a difference at least this big anyway? If the answer is below one in twenty, the result is called statistically significant.
D
That threshold is a convention. It was not derived; it was chosen, and it could have been one in fifty or one in ten without anything in nature changing.
E

A study of two hundred thousand people can find a statistically significant difference that is far too small to be worth acting on. A study of twelve people can miss a large and real effect and report no significant difference.
F

This is why a headline reading SIGNIFICANT DROP IN RISK is almost unreadable on its own. It may mean the drop is unlikely to be chance, which is a claim about the statistics, and not about the size of the drop.
G

The word has not been misused by the scientists. It has been borrowed by headline writers from a field where it has a technical meaning, and dropped into a sentence where readers supply the everyday one.

title: Mistakes Were Made

p: A
English lets a writer build a sentence that names an action without naming whoever performed it. The window was broken. The order was given. Mistakes were made.
B

This is the passive voice with the actor removed. It is not a fault in itself: a scientist writing the sample was heated to 90 degrees is using it because the identity of whoever did the heating is genuinely beside the point.
C

In an official report the same construction does other work. Funds were misallocated tells a reader that money went where it should not have gone and withholds the one fact a reader most wants, which is by whom.
D

Compare two sentences carrying the same facts. The inspector did not visit the site for three years names a person and an omission. Inspections were not carried out names neither, and the second is what tends to appear in print.
E

The effect is not only about blame. A sentence with no actor is also a sentence with nothing to fix. If inspections were not carried out, the problem is a process; if an inspector did not visit, the problem is a job somebody holds.
F
Readers can test a document quickly. Take any sentence describing something going wrong and ask whether a person or an organization appears as the subject, and keep count across a page.
G

Writers are not always hiding. Sometimes the actor is unknown, and sometimes naming one person for a failure shared by many would be its own distortion. The question is whether the pattern holds everywhere in a document or only where the news is bad.

Summarize what the agentless passive does in an official report.

A sentence like funds were misallocated names an action without naming who performed it, so it withholds the fact a reader most wants. It also leaves nothing to fix, because a process is at fault rather than a job somebody holds, and readers can test a document by asking whether a person appears as the subject where the news is bad.
vocabulary

passive voice: a sentence form in which the thing acted on becomes the subject, as in the order was given.
agentless: here, a passive sentence that never says who performed the action.
connection
Describe the connection between naming an actor and being able to fix a problem.

If inspections were not carried out the problem is a process, and if an inspector did not visit the site the problem is a job somebody holds, so a sentence with no actor is a sentence with nothing to fix.
note: Give students a real report and have them count. The test in paragraph F is the lesson, i.e. whether the pattern holds everywhere or only where the news is bad.

title: What a Doctor Means by Positive

p: A

A positive test result sounds like bad news and a negative one like good news, and in a clinic the words carry neither meaning. Positive means the test detected what it looks for. Negative means it did not.
B
No test detects perfectly. Two numbers describe how a test fails: how often it misses the thing when the thing is there, and how often it reports the thing when the thing is absent.
C
The second kind of failure is the one that surprises people. A test can be ninety-nine per cent accurate in the ordinary sense and still produce more wrong positives than right ones.
D

Suppose a condition affects one person in ten thousand, and a million people are tested. About a hundred of them have it. If the test wrongly flags one healthy person in a hundred, that is roughly ten thousand false positives.
E

So of everyone told they tested positive, the great majority do not have the condition. Nothing is wrong with the test. The arithmetic depends on how rare the condition is, which is a fact about the population and not about the test.
F
This is why a result is usually described as a screen rather than a diagnosis, and why a positive screen is followed by a second and different test rather than by treatment.
G

The everyday meanings of the words make all of this harder to explain. A patient hearing positive hears a verdict, when the clinician said only that one instrument responded, and said nothing yet about what is true.

title: The Words on a Census Form

p: A
A census looks like an act of counting, and counting looks like the plainest thing a government can do. The form, though, is a list of words, and each word decides what can be counted at all.
B

A question offering a fixed list of boxes can only return the categories on the list. A person whose situation is not on it either picks the nearest box or is recorded as other, and both outcomes change the total.
C

Categories also change between censuses. The wording used for a household, for an occupation, for a family relationship has been rewritten many times, and each rewrite breaks the comparison with the census before it.
D

That is not carelessness. A category that no longer matches how people actually live produces numbers that are precise and useless, so the words have to be revised, and revising them has a cost that is paid in continuity.
E
The stakes are real, because census counts are not only descriptions. They are used to draw electoral boundaries, to distribute funding and to decide where a hospital or a school is built.
F

So a change of wording is a political event as well as a technical one. Hearings are held about single questions, and the arguments are about who will appear in the resulting figures and who will not.
G
Reading an old census well means reading its form first. The number in a column answers the question that was printed, which is often not the question a modern reader assumes it answers.

Summarize why the wording on a census form matters.

title: What Natural Means on a Label

p: A

Two words on a food package can look like a matched pair and work completely differently. Organic is defined in regulation, with rules about what may be used in growing and processing, and an inspection behind the claim.
B

Natural, in the United States, has no comparable definition for most foods. A manufacturer using it is making a claim that no specific standard sits behind, which is why the same word can appear on products made in very different ways.
C
Readers supply the missing meaning themselves. Natural carries a strong connotation of unprocessed, of grown rather than made, and that connotation does the work a definition would otherwise do.
D

Neither word is a measure of nutrition. An organic biscuit and a conventional biscuit are both biscuits, and the certification describes how the ingredients were produced rather than what they do in a body.
E

Some terms are defined in a narrower way than readers expect. A claim about serving size, for instance, is measured against a serving the manufacturer states, which may be smaller than anyone eats at one sitting.
F

The useful habit is to move from the front of the package to the back. The front is designed and the words on it are chosen; the ingredient list and the nutrition panel are formats a regulator specifies.
G
None of this makes the front of the package a lie. It makes it an advertisement, which is a different kind of writing with a different purpose, and reading it as though it were a report is the error.

How do the words organic and natural differ on a package in the United States?
Organic is defined in regulation with rules about growing and processing and an inspection behind the claim, while natural has no comparable definition for most foods.

Paragraph C (i.e. readers supplying the meaning themselves) and paragraph F (i.e. moving from the front of the package to the back).
summarize
Summarize why the front of a food package should be read differently from the back.

Describe the connection between a word having no definition and readers trusting it anyway.

title: The Inverted Pyramid

p: A
Most stories told out loud build toward their ending. A news report does the opposite. It puts the outcome in the first sentence and then works backwards into detail, context and quotation.
B
The shape has a name. It is called the inverted pyramid, because the widest and heaviest material sits at the top and the paragraphs narrow in importance as they go down.
C

The habit is usually traced to the telegraph. A wire could fail mid-message and transmission was charged by the word, so a correspondent who buried the outcome risked sending the least useful part of the story first.
D
A second pressure came from the page. An editor fitting stories into a fixed column cut from the bottom, and a story written as a pyramid could lose its last three paragraphs and still make sense.
E

The structure shapes what a reader takes away. Someone who reads only the opening gets the outcome and no qualification, and the conditions, the uncertainties and the dissenting voice all live further down.
F
That is why two readers of the same article can disagree about what it said. They did not read the same amount of it, and the parts they missed are the parts carrying the hedges.
G
Online the shape is loosening, because a page has no bottom to cut from. Some outlets now use a chronological or a question-and-answer form, and the reader has to work out which shape they are in.

Why did an editor's habit of cutting from the bottom reward the inverted pyramid?

Paragraph E (i.e. what a reader of only the opening misses) and paragraph G (i.e. how the shape is loosening online).
summarize
Summarize the inverted pyramid and what it does to readers.

inverted pyramid: the news structure in which the most important material comes first and importance narrows downward.
connection
Describe the connection between where the hedges sit and readers disagreeing about an article.
Someone who reads only the opening gets the outcome and no qualification, so two readers can disagree because the parts they missed are the parts carrying the hedges.
note: RI.7.5 asks how sections contribute to the whole. Have students cut a real article after paragraph two and describe what claim they are now left holding.

title: Why a Field Guide Is Not Alphabetical

p: A
A dictionary is alphabetical because a reader already knows the word. A field guide cannot be, because a reader holding an unknown leaf has nothing to look it up under.
B

So a guide is organized by what can be observed. Trees are grouped by leaf arrangement and shape, birds by silhouette and habitat, rocks by hardness and lustre, and the organization is the first half of the identification.
C
Many guides go further and provide a key. A key is a chain of paired choices: leaves opposite or alternate, edge toothed or smooth, and each answer sends the reader to another pair.
D
Each step removes roughly half the possibilities. A set of six or seven choices can therefore separate one species out of a hundred, which is far quicker than reading a hundred descriptions.
E
The design has a cost. A key only works if every choice can be answered from the specimen in hand, so a key built on flowers is useless in November and one built on bark is uncertain on a young tree.
F
Good guides handle that by offering more than one route in, such as a winter key and a summer key, and by admitting where a pair of species cannot be separated on what a reader can see outdoors.
G
The organization is therefore an argument about how identification happens. The order of the pages is a claim that these features, in this sequence, are the ones a person in a field can actually use.

Paragraph D (i.e. how a key narrows the possibilities) and paragraph E (i.e. the cost of building a key on one feature).

Summarize how a field guide is organized and why.

key: a chain of paired either-or choices that leads a reader to an identification.
specimen: the individual plant, animal or rock a person actually has in front of them.

Describe the connection between each choice removing half the possibilities and the number of steps a key needs.

title: The Shape of a Court Opinion

p: A
A written court opinion is not organized like an argument someone would make out loud. It has fixed parts in a fixed order, and knowing the order tells a reader what each passage is for.
B

It usually opens with the facts, told flatly. Who did what, when, and what the lower courts decided. This section is meant to be uncontroversial, and where the parties disagree about a fact the opinion says so.
C
Then comes the question presented, narrowed as far as the court can narrow it. A case about a search is not decided as a case about privacy in general, and the narrowing is deliberate.
D
The holding is the answer to that question, and it is the part that binds other courts. It is often a single sentence, and it is often shorter than readers expect.
E

The reasoning follows, and it is the longest part. It walks through earlier decisions, statutes and the consequences of ruling each way, and it has to explain why the earlier cases point where the court says they point.
F
A dissent is printed after. Its author lost, so the dissent binds nobody, and its purpose is to mark exactly where the disagreement lies rather than to restate the whole dispute.
G

Reading the parts in order prevents a common error. A sentence quoted from the reasoning, or worse from the dissent, is often repeated as though it were the holding, which is the one part that actually decided anything.

Summarize the parts of a court opinion and what each is for.

title: The Order of a Checklist

p: A

In October 1935 the United States Army Air Corps watched a new Boeing bomber take off at Wright Field, climb, stall and crash. Two of the crew died, including the pilot, who was among the most experienced in the service.
B

The aircraft was sound. A gust lock, which holds the control surfaces still on the ground, had been left engaged, and the pilot had simply not got to it among everything else the new machine required.
C
The conclusion at the time was that the design was too much aeroplane for one man to fly. The response was not to simplify the aeroplane. It was to write down the steps.
D

A checklist is not a set of instructions, and the difference matters. Instructions teach somebody who does not know how; a checklist catches somebody who knows perfectly well and is going to miss one item anyway.
E
So its structure is unusual. Items are short, they are stated as actions with a confirming response, and there are few of them, because a list long enough to be thorough is long enough to be skipped.
F
The order is not arbitrary either. Items are grouped by pause points in the task, such as before starting engines or before takeoff, so the list is read at a moment when stopping costs nothing.
G
The same form has since been taken into operating theatres and construction. What travelled was not the aviation content but the structure, which is the part that does the work.

title: Why a Treaty Has a Preamble

p: A

A treaty opens with a passage that promises nothing. It names the parties, recalls earlier agreements and states what the signatories are trying to achieve, in sentences that often begin with desiring or recognising.
B
Readers skip it, reasonably enough, because the obligations are further down. The articles that follow are numbered, and each one states something a party must do, must not do, or may do.
C
The preamble still does work, and the work shows up later. When two governments disagree about what an article means, the stated purpose becomes part of how the article is read.
D
That is not an informal custom. The international rules on interpreting treaties direct an interpreter to read a term in its context, and they define that context to include the preamble.
E
Which is why the preamble is argued over in negotiation. A word there costs nothing today and may decide a dispute in twenty years, so delegations fight about language that appears to bind nobody.
F

The structure also separates the kinds of commitment. Aspiration goes at the top where it cannot be enforced, and obligation goes into numbered articles where it can, and a reader can tell which is which by location alone.
G
Treating the preamble as decoration therefore misreads the document. It is the part that says what the rest is for, placed where a lawyer can reach it when the text alone runs out.

title: Who Paid for the Study

p: A
At the end of a research paper there is usually a short paragraph nobody reads. It says who funded the work and whether any author has a financial interest in the result.
B

The paragraph exists because funding is known to shift findings. Across many fields, studies paid for by an industry reach conclusions favourable to that industry more often than independently funded studies of the same question.
C

The reason is rarely fraud. A funder influences which questions get asked, which comparison a new product is tested against, how long a trial runs and whether a study that came out badly is published at all.
D
A reader who treats the disclosure as a verdict gets it wrong in the other direction. Industry funds a great deal of genuine research, and a study is not refuted by who paid for it.
E

What the disclosure does is tell a reader where to look harder. It is a reason to check the comparison group, the length of the trial and whether the measure reported is the one the study originally set out to measure.
F
Good authors go further and say so themselves. A paper may state that a funder had no role in the design or in the decision to publish, which is a claim the authors are putting their names behind.
G
So the paragraph is not an accusation and not a clearance. It is information about the position the work was written from, offered so that a reader can weigh it rather than guess at it.

B
The paragraph exists because funding shifts findings. In many fields, studies paid for by an industry favour that industry more often than independent studies of the same question.
C
The reason is rarely fraud. A funder shapes which questions are asked. It shapes what a product is compared against, how long a trial runs, and whether a bad result is published.
D
A reader who treats the disclosure as a verdict goes wrong the other way. Industry funds much real research. A study is not refuted by who paid for it.
E
What the disclosure does is show where to look harder. Check the comparison group. Check the length of the trial. Check whether the measure reported is the one they set out to measure.
F
Good authors say more. A paper may state that the funder had no role in the design or in the choice to publish. The authors put their names behind that claim.
G
So the paragraph is not an accusation. It is not a clearance either. It is information about where the work was written from. A reader can weigh it instead of guessing.

How does a funder usually influence a result, according to the article?
Rarely by fraud, but by influencing which questions get asked, which comparison a product is tested against, how long a trial runs and whether a study that came out badly is published at all.
paragraph focus
Paragraph D (i.e. why a disclosure is not a verdict) and paragraph E (i.e. what a reader should check instead).
summarize
Summarize what a funding disclosure tells a reader.

It says who paid for the work and whether an author gains from the result, and it exists because industry-funded studies more often favour that industry. It is not a refutation, because industry funds genuine research, so what it offers is a reason to check the comparison group, the length of the trial and whether the reported measure is the original one.
vocabulary

disclosure: a statement revealing an interest that a reader would want to know about.
comparison group: what a new treatment is tested against, which a funder may influence.
connection
Describe the connection between knowing who funded a study and knowing where to look harder.

Because a funder influences the comparison, the length of the trial and whether a bad result is published, the disclosure tells a reader to check those things rather than to accept or reject the study.
note: RI.7.6 asks how an author marks their own position against others. Paragraph F is that move in miniature, i.e. the authors stating the funder had no role.

title: The Plaque That Was Replaced

p: A
A monument usually carries a small plaque, and the plaque is a piece of writing with an author, a date and a purpose, even though it rarely names any of the three.
B

A plaque written in 1910 and a plaque written in 2010 about the same event will differ in more than tone. They differ in what they treat as needing explanation and in who the sentences assume is reading.
C

An older text often uses the passive voice and words such as settled or pacified. A newer one more often names the parties, gives numbers, and states who died, which is a choice about what counts as the event.
D
Where a plaque has been replaced, some sites keep the old one mounted beside the new. The pairing lets a visitor compare, and it also makes the first plaque into an exhibit rather than a statement.
E

Replacement is argued about, and the arguments are not only about history. One side says a text that misdescribes an event should be corrected like any other error. The other says removing it hides that the misdescription was once official.
F

A careful new plaque does something that answers both. It states the event, and then it states what the earlier plaque said and when, which distinguishes the position it is taking from the position it replaced.
G
That is the move worth noticing. Any writer can assert. Marking where your account differs from an earlier one, and saying so on the same panel, is a harder and more useful thing to do.

Paragraph E (i.e. the argument about replacing a plaque) and paragraph F (i.e. what a careful new plaque does).
summarize
Summarize the argument about replacing a plaque and how a new one can answer it.

exhibit: something displayed to be examined, rather than a statement a visitor is asked to accept.

title: The Choices in a Nature Film

p: A
A nature documentary presents itself as a window. The camera appears simply to have been there, and the animals appear to be doing what they would have done anyway.
B
Much of that is true, and the patience behind it is real. A sequence of a few minutes can rest on months in a hide, and the behaviour on screen is behaviour that happened.
C

The sound is a different matter. Microphones cannot usually record a small animal at a distance over wind, so footsteps, wingbeats and rustling are commonly created afterwards in a studio and matched to the picture.
D
The score does more than fill silence. Music tells a viewer whether a hunt is a tragedy or a triumph, and the same footage of the same hunt can be cut to make either, without a single frame changing.
E

Narration carries a position too. Calling an animal a mother rather than a female, or saying it is determined rather than that it continued, invites a viewer to read intention into behaviour nobody can ask about.
F
None of this is deception by itself. A film has to choose a sound, a score and a sentence, and refusing to choose is not available; silence and a flat voice are choices as well.
G
What a viewer can do is notice the choosing. Watching a sequence once with the sound off is usually enough, because the story the pictures tell alone is frequently a looser and less certain one.

Summarize the choices a nature film makes and why noticing them matters.

title: The Editorial and the News Story

p: A
A newspaper prints two kinds of writing about the same events and signals the difference in ways a hurried reader can miss. One kind reports. The other argues, and is supposed to say so.
B
A news story is built to be checkable. Claims are attributed, the people criticised are offered a reply, and the reporter's own view is meant not to appear in the sentences at all.
C
An editorial drops all three constraints on purpose. It takes a position, it is unsigned because it speaks for the paper rather than a person, and it is placed on a page set aside for that.
D
The signals are physical as well. A different column width, a standing label, a box, sometimes a different typeface, all of which say to a reader that the rules just changed.
E
Online, almost all of that disappears. A link shared in a message arrives without the page, without the column width and often without the label, and both kinds of writing look identical on a phone.
F

So the work falls to the reader, and there are quick tests. Are claims attributed to someone who could be asked? Does anyone disagreeing get quoted? Is the writer named, and does the piece recommend something?
G

An editorial is not a lesser thing than a report. A paper arguing openly for a position, over its own name, is doing something honest. The difficulty is only that the frame around it has been stripped off.

What three constraints does an editorial drop on purpose?

paragraph focus
Paragraph D (i.e. the physical signals on a printed page) and paragraph E (i.e. what happens to those signals online).
summarize
Summarize the difference between a news story and an editorial and why it is harder to see online.

A news story attributes claims, offers a reply to those criticised and keeps the reporter's view out, while an editorial takes a position, is unsigned and sits on its own page. Print marks the difference with column width, labels and typeface, and a link shared on a phone arrives without any of that, so a reader has to test for attribution, quoted disagreement and a recommendation.
vocabulary

attribute: to say who a claim comes from, so a reader could go and ask them.
editorial: an unsigned piece arguing a position on behalf of the publication rather than a person.
connection
Describe the connection between losing the page and losing the signal.
A link shared in a message arrives without the page, the column width and often the label, so both kinds of writing look identical and the reader has to test the piece instead.
note: The four tests in paragraph F are the takeaway. Run them on one shared link in class and see which of the four it fails.

title: The Paragraph Where an Author Admits the Limits

p: A
Near the end of a research paper there is usually a section headed limitations. It is written by the authors, about their own work, and it lists the reasons their conclusion might be wrong.
B

That is an unusual thing for any writer to do. Most writing argues for its claim and leaves the weaknesses for an opponent to find, and a section volunteering them looks at first like a tactical error.
C
It is not. A paper that names its weaknesses is telling a reader where its claim stops, and a claim with a stated edge is more useful than one that appears to apply everywhere.
D

The section also marks the author's position against other work. Saying that a sample was drawn from one city distinguishes this paper from one claiming a national result, without having to criticise the other paper directly.
E

A reader can judge the section itself. A good one names limits that actually threaten the conclusion. A weak one lists things that sound humble and change nothing, such as calling for further research.
F

The absence of such a section is informative too. Press releases and advertisements never include one, and that is the clearest difference between a document reporting a result and a document selling it.
G
So the paragraph most readers skip is the one that shows most about how a text was written. It is where an author draws a line around their own claim rather than waiting for somebody else to draw it.

Summarize what a limitations section does.

note: Pair this with a press release about the same finding. The comparison in paragraph F does the teaching by itself.

title: The Speech on the Page and in the Air

p: A

A speech exists twice. There is a text, which can be read in silence at any speed, and there is a delivery, which happened once, at a particular pace, in a particular room, in front of people who answered back.
B
The text is the version that gets quoted and taught. It can be searched, marked up and compared, and every reader of it receives exactly the same words in exactly the same order.
C

The recording carries what the page cannot hold. Pace, volume, the length of a pause, a voice that tightens or steadies, and the sound of an audience responding, which changes what the next sentence has to do.
D
Sometimes the two versions are not even the same words. Speakers cut, repeat and add, and the most remembered passage of a speech is occasionally one that was not in the prepared text at all.
E

Martin Luther King's address in Washington in 1963 is the familiar example. The closing section that nearly everyone can name was not in the typed draft, and the recording is the only evidence of how it arrived.
F
This matters for how a claim gets studied. A historian comparing a draft, a delivered recording and a newspaper transcript of the same speech has three documents, and they will not agree.
G
Neither version is the real one. The text is what was planned and the recording is what happened, and a reader who has only met one of them has met half of the event.

Summarize why a speech has to be studied in more than one form.

title: Three Ways to Look at a Heart

p: A

A doctor listening through a stethoscope is reading a heart by sound. Valves closing make the two familiar beats, and a sound that does not belong, such as a murmur, suggests blood moving where it should not.
B
Sound is immediate and cheap, and it is also crude. It tells a listener that something is irregular long before it tells them what, and two different problems can produce a similar noise.
C
An electrocardiogram records something else entirely. It is not sound but electrical activity, drawn as a line, and it shows the timing and the sequence of the signal that makes the muscle contract.
D
That makes it excellent for rhythm and nearly blind to structure. A trace can show that the signal is arriving in the wrong order while saying nothing about whether a valve is thickened.
E

An echocardiogram uses ultrasound to build a moving picture. It shows the chambers filling and emptying and the valves opening, which is the structural question the first two instruments cannot answer.
F
Each instrument is a different medium reporting on the same organ, and each is strongest exactly where the others are weak. A clinician choosing between them is choosing what kind of question to ask.
G
The same holds outside medicine. A table, a photograph and a recording of one event are not three copies of it, and deciding which to trust means first deciding what you are trying to find out.

title: The Night the Radio Play Aired

p: A
On the evening of October 30, 1938, a radio drama adapted H. G. Wells's novel about a Martian invasion. The company broadcast it as a series of news bulletins interrupting a music programme.
B

The form was the point. A listener tuning in late heard what sounded like an announcer breaking into a dance band with reports from New Jersey, and the dramatic structure borrowed the authority of a medium people trusted.
C

The next morning's newspapers described a nation in panic. Headlines reported crowds in the streets, people fleeing cities and switchboards overwhelmed, and that account entered textbooks and stayed there.
D

Later research questioned nearly all of it. The programme had a small audience that night, surveys taken immediately afterwards found few listeners who believed an invasion was underway, and the widespread flight is poorly evidenced.
E
There are also reasons why newspapers would tell it that way. Radio was taking advertising revenue from print, and a story about a reckless new medium frightening the public served the older one.
F

So there are three things to compare: a novel, a broadcast that changed the novel's form without changing its plot, and a press account of the broadcast that may say more about newspapers than about listeners.
G
The lesson is not that nobody was alarmed, because some people clearly were. It is that the size of a reaction is a claim like any other, and it needs evidence that is not simply another headline.

title: A Bird Call in Three Forms

p: A
Older field guides describe a bird's song in words. A phrase such as a clear whistled three-note call, falling at the end, is a sentence doing a job that sentences are not well suited to.
B

Some guides use mnemonics instead, inventing English words that sound like the song. These are memorable and they are also a trap, because once a listener has learned one, the bird begins to sound like the phrase.
C
A recording solves the obvious problem and creates a new one. It is exact, but it is gone as soon as it is played, and a listener cannot hold the beginning of a song beside the end of it.
D

A spectrogram is the third form. Time runs across the page, pitch runs up it, and the energy of the sound is drawn as marks, so a song that lasts two seconds becomes a shape that can be examined for as long as you like.
E
The shape shows things the ear struggles with. Two songs that sound alike can have clearly different slopes, and a note too fast to count by ear appears as four separate marks on the page.
F
No form is complete. The description is portable, the recording is faithful, the spectrogram is analysable, and birders in practice use all three in the same morning.
G

That is why modern guides print spectrograms beside the text and link to recordings. The guide is not offering the same information three times; it is offering three things that each survive a different kind of use.

title: When a Trial Is Televised

p: A

A court produces a written record of everything said in it. A transcript is complete, in order, and dull, and for most of history it was the only way the public could learn what happened in a room they were not in.
B

Cameras change the available evidence. A viewer sees hesitation, posture and whether a witness looked at the person they were accusing, none of which the transcript records and some of which jurors are told to weigh.
C

That is the argument in favour. Proceedings are supposed to be public, a transcript is public only to people who will read two hundred pages, and a broadcast is public in a way an ordinary person can actually use.
D

The argument against is that a camera is not a window. Coverage is edited, the minute selected for a news bulletin is chosen because something happened in it, and hours of procedure are what a trial mostly is.
E
There is also an effect on the room. Lawyers, witnesses and judges who know they are being recorded behave differently, and a system that depends on candid testimony has reason to worry about that.
F

Different courts have settled this differently. Some allow cameras, some allow audio only, some allow sketch artists and nothing else, and each rule is a judgement about which record does least damage.
G

A student comparing a clip with the transcript of the same hour is doing the whole exercise. The question is not which is accurate, because both are, but what each medium selects and what it leaves out.

title: The Argument for a Later School Start

p: A

The case for starting secondary school later runs like this. Adolescent sleep timing shifts later for biological reasons, a start before eight o'clock cuts sleep rather than moving it, and short sleep damages learning, mood and safety.
B
The first claim is the strongest. The shift in timing at puberty has been measured in laboratories and across many countries, and it is not explained away by phones or by homework.
C
The second follows reasonably. If the body clock has moved and the alarm has not, the hours are taken off the front of the night, and surveys of teenagers consistently show exactly that pattern.
D

The third claim is where the evidence gets mixed. Studies of districts that moved their start times report gains in attendance and in reported sleep, and the findings on grades are smaller and less consistent.
E
One result is often quoted on its own: a fall in teenage car crashes after a district moved its start. That study is real, but a single district over a few years is a thin base for a general claim.
F

There is also a cost side the argument sometimes skips. Bus schedules, after-school work, sport and the care of younger siblings all move with the bell, and those effects fall unevenly across families.
G
The argument is therefore strong at its foundation and weaker at its edges. A reader who accepts the biology is not thereby obliged to accept every number attached to it.

Summarize the argument for a later start and where its evidence weakens.

title: The Case Against the New Stadium

p: A
A city is asked to help pay for a stadium, and the proposal arrives with an economic impact study. The study projects jobs, visitor spending and tax revenue, and the numbers are large.
B
Such studies are usually commissioned by the party that wants the stadium, which does not make them wrong but does tell a reader which assumptions to check first.
C

The main objection economists raise is substitution. Money a local family spends at a game is mostly money it would otherwise have spent on something else in the same city, so the regional total moves far less than the gross figure suggests.
D

A second objection concerns the jobs. Stadium employment is heavily part-time and seasonal, and a headline counting positions rather than full-time equivalents can describe the same work several times over.
E

A third concerns what the money could have done instead. A subsidy spent on a stadium is not available for a bus route or a school roof, and a fair comparison is against that alternative, not against nothing.
F
The case in favour is not empty. A stadium can anchor a district that was emptying, and a city may reasonably decide that having a team is worth paying for as a civic good rather than an investment.
G

That is the distinction the argument turns on. Saying a stadium will pay for itself is a claim about economics that the evidence mostly does not support. Saying it is worth having anyway is a different claim, and an honest one.

title: The Argument for Culling the Deer

p: A

A park proposes to reduce its deer population by shooting. The argument offered is ecological: the herd has no large predators, numbers have risen, and the browsing is preventing the forest from regenerating.
B

The regeneration claim can be tested directly. Fencing a plot excludes deer, and if seedlings grow inside the fence and not outside it, the deer are the explanation rather than soil, light or rainfall.
C

Exclosure studies of that kind are strong evidence, and they are also local. A result from one plot in one forest supports a claim about that forest and not automatically about a park two counties away.
D
The argument's second step is weaker in an interesting way. Showing that deer are causing the damage does not by itself show that this cull, at this size, at this time of year, will fix it.
E

Opponents propose alternatives, including fertility control, fencing valuable areas and reintroducing predators. Each has an evidence base, and each works at a different scale and over a different timescale.
F

The arguments that are hardest to assess are the ones not made in ecological terms at all. Objections about shooting in a public park, or about what a park is for, are real positions, and an impact study cannot settle them.
G
A careful reader sorts the claims before judging them: what is measured, what is predicted, and what is a value. Mixing the three is what makes these disputes feel unresolvable when they are not.

Summarize the argument for a cull and how a reader should assess it.

title: The Claim That Scores Fell

p: A
A headline reports that reading scores have fallen. Before the explanations begin, a reader has several questions, and the answers decide whether there is anything to explain.
B
The first is who was tested. If more students sat the test this year, including students who would not have sat it before, the average can fall while no individual student has got worse.
C

The second is whether the test changed. A revised test is not the old test, and comparing a score from one with a score from the other requires a statistical bridge that may or may not have been built.
D
The third is what the line is measured against. A score can fall relative to last year, relative to a decade ago, or relative to a standard that somebody set, and those are three different claims.
E
The fourth is the size of the change. Test scores move slightly every year for reasons nobody can name, and a change inside that ordinary range is not a trend no matter how it is reported.
F
None of these questions is a reason to dismiss the report. Sometimes scores really do fall, and an article that answers all four and still reports a drop has made its case.
G

The habit worth building is the order of operations. Establish that the change is real before arguing about its cause, because a confident explanation of a change that did not happen is worse than no explanation.

Summarize the four questions to ask about a report that scores fell.

title: The Claim About Plastic Straws

p: A

Campaigns to ban plastic straws spread quickly, helped by a video of a turtle with a straw lodged in its nostril. The argument was that straws are unnecessary, replaceable and harmful, and all three are defensible.
B

The weak link is scale. By weight, straws are a very small share of the plastic entering the ocean, and the large contributors are discarded fishing gear and waste escaping from a relatively small number of rivers.
C
That does not make a ban pointless. Harm is not only a question of mass, a light object can kill an animal that swallows it, and an item nobody needs is an easy thing to stop producing.
D
It does make one particular sentence false. A campaign claiming that banning straws will substantially reduce ocean plastic is making a quantitative claim, and the quantities do not support it.
E

Supporters often shift ground when pressed, and the second argument is more interesting than the first. Straws are a starting point, the claim goes, and a person who changes one habit becomes easier to persuade about larger ones.
F

That is a claim about psychology rather than about plastic, and it has its own evidence, which is mixed. Some studies find a small action increases later commitment, others find it substitutes for one.
G
So the honest version of the campaign is narrower and harder to put on a poster. It says straws are a cheap thing to stop doing and that the main sources lie elsewhere and are harder to reach.

Paragraph C (i.e. why a ban is not pointless) and paragraph F (i.e. the mixed evidence about small actions).

Describe the connection between harm and mass in this argument.
