title: Two Accounts of the Dust Bowl

p: A

In the 1930s the southern plains of the United States lost a great deal of their topsoil to the wind. Dust storms darkened the sky as far east as the Atlantic coast, and families abandoned farms across several states.
B

A government film made in 1936 presented the disaster as the result of ploughing. Native grass had held the soil through dry years for a very long time, the argument ran, and the plough removed what the drought then exposed.
C

The evidence for that account is agricultural. Wheat acreage on the plains expanded enormously during and after the First World War, and the land that blew was overwhelmingly land that had been broken.
D

Many people who lived there told it differently. Their accounts emphasise the drought itself, which was severe and prolonged, and the fact that farmers had been encouraged by government, by railroads and by prices to plough exactly where they ploughed.
E

The evidence for that account is also real. Rainfall records show a genuine extreme, and the promotional literature urging settlement on the plains was produced by the same institutions that later explained what went wrong.
F

The two accounts do not disagree about many facts. They disagree about which facts are the centre of the story, and therefore about whether this was a natural event made worse by farming or a farming event made visible by weather.
G
A reader comparing them should notice what each leaves at the edges. The film is thin on who encouraged the ploughing; the local accounts are thin on what ploughing did. Neither gap is an accident.

What evidence supports the account that blames ploughing?

title: Two Papers on One Fossil

p: A
In 2003 a team excavating a cave on the Indonesian island of Flores found a small skeleton. The individual had stood about a metre tall and had a brain roughly a third the size of a modern human's.
B

The first paper described a new species. Its evidence was the proportions of the limbs, the shape of the wrist bones and the pelvis, and the fact that the remains were dated to a period when modern humans were already in the region.
C

A second group published a different reading of the same bones. In their account the skeleton was a modern human affected by a condition that reduces growth and brain size, and the unusual features were pathology rather than ancestry.
D

Both papers cited measurements, and in several cases the same measurements. The disagreement was about which features are diagnostic: a wrist bone that develops early is harder to explain as illness than overall body size is.
E

Evidence accumulated that favoured the first reading. More individuals were found at the site, which is difficult to explain if the first was a single affected person, and stone tools in the deposit covered a long span of time.
F

The second group did not simply concede, and that is normal. A claim is usually abandoned gradually as new evidence makes it more expensive to maintain, rather than at a moment when someone announces they were wrong.
G
Reading both papers side by side teaches more than reading the winner. The same bones supported two accounts, and what settled it was not argument but material that neither team had when they wrote.

title: The Two Texts of a Treaty

p: A
The Treaty of Waitangi was signed in New Zealand in 1840. It exists in two versions, one in English and one in Māori, and the difference between them has shaped the country's law ever since.
B
The English text has Māori chiefs ceding sovereignty to the Crown. That is a strong word in English law, and it describes the transfer of the ultimate authority to govern.
C

The Māori text uses kāwanatanga, a word built from the transliteration of governor. It conveys something closer to governorship than to sovereignty, and it is not the word a Māori speaker would have reached for to mean full authority.
D

The same Māori text then guarantees the chiefs tino rangatiratanga over their lands and treasures. That phrase does carry the sense of full authority, which produces a document promising in one clause what the other appears to take.
E
Almost all of the roughly five hundred signatures were made on the Māori text. That matters, because the people signing were agreeing to the document in front of them and in their own language.
F

Historians differ on how deliberate the gap was. Some read it as the haste and imprecision of a translation made overnight; others point out that the translator knew both languages well and that the softer word served the Crown's purpose.
G
Modern practice does not pick one text and discard the other. It asks what the parties understood themselves to be agreeing to, which is a question the existence of two texts makes unavoidable.

Historians differ on how deliberate the gap was. Some call it haste in an overnight translation. Others note the translator knew both languages well, and the softer word suited the Crown.
G
Modern practice does not pick one text and drop the other. It asks what the parties understood they were agreeing to. Two texts make that question unavoidable.

Why does the Māori text appear to promise in one clause what another takes?
It uses kāwanatanga, which is closer to governorship than sovereignty, and then guarantees the chiefs tino rangatiratanga over their lands and treasures, which does carry the sense of full authority.
paragraph focus
Paragraph E (i.e. which text was actually signed) and paragraph F (i.e. how historians differ about the gap).
summarize
Summarize why the Treaty of Waitangi has two texts and why it matters.

The English text has chiefs ceding sovereignty, while the Māori text uses kāwanatanga, closer to governorship, and then guarantees tino rangatiratanga, which means full authority. Almost all the signatures were on the Māori text, historians differ over whether the gap was haste or purpose, and modern practice asks what the parties understood rather than choosing one text.
vocabulary

cede: to give up or hand over, used in the English text for the transfer of sovereignty.
transliteration: writing a word from one language in the letters and sounds of another, as kāwanatanga is built from governor.
connection
Describe the connection between which text was signed and how the treaty is read today.

Almost all of the roughly five hundred signatures were made on the Māori text, and the people signing were agreeing to the document in front of them in their own language, so modern practice asks what the parties understood themselves to be agreeing to.
note: Two authors, one event, two documents, and the difference is a single word in each. This is the sharpest RI.7.9 example in the set.

title: Why the Big Animals Vanished

p: A

At the end of the last ice age, most of the very large land mammals disappeared. Mammoths, giant ground sloths and others vanished from several continents within a span that is short by geological standards.
B

One explanation puts the cause on people. Extinctions on each landmass tend to follow the arrival of modern humans, the pattern repeats on islands reached much later, and the species lost are overwhelmingly large and slow-breeding.
C

The other explanation puts the cause on climate. The end of the ice age reorganised vegetation across whole continents, and an animal adapted to one kind of grassland does not simply move when the grassland changes composition.
D

Each account emphasises evidence the other treats as secondary. The first points at timing and at island cases; the second points at pollen records and at species that disappeared where hunting evidence is scarce.
E

Africa is the case both must address. It lost proportionally fewer large mammals than other continents, and each explanation has an answer, which is that its animals evolved alongside humans or that its climate shifted less.
F
The disagreement has narrowed over time, and most researchers now argue for a combination in which small populations under climate stress were finished by hunting they could otherwise have absorbed.
G

A combined answer is not a compromise for the sake of peace. It is what the evidence supports, and it is harder to state than either original claim, which is one reason the simpler versions persist in print.

What evidence supports the explanation that blames people?

paragraph focus
Paragraph E (i.e. how each explanation handles Africa) and paragraph G (i.e. why a combined answer is not a compromise).
summarize
Summarize the two explanations for the loss of the large mammals.

One account blames people, citing extinctions following human arrival, the same pattern on islands, and the loss of large slow-breeding species. The other blames climate, citing the reorganisation of vegetation and pollen records. Both must explain why Africa lost proportionally fewer, and most researchers now argue that climate stress left small populations that hunting finished.
vocabulary

pollen record: preserved pollen in sediments, used to show what plants grew in a place at a given time.
connection
Describe the connection between climate stress and hunting in the combined explanation.
Small populations already under climate stress were finished by hunting they could otherwise have absorbed.
note: Students often want a winner. The useful question is what each side would accept as a decisive observation, which is harder and more honest.

title: Two Histories of One Strike

p: A

In 1892 the steelworks at Homestead, Pennsylvania locked out its union workers over a wage dispute. The company brought in three hundred armed Pinkerton agents by barge, and the fighting that followed killed men on both sides.
B

A history written from company records describes a firm protecting property. In that account the workers seized the plant, the agents were guards hired to restore lawful access, and the violence began when the barges were fired on.
C

A history written from union records and local newspapers describes a town defending itself. In that account the company had planned the lockout for months, the agents arrived armed at four in the morning, and the townspeople were resisting an invasion.
D

Both accounts can cite documents. Company correspondence shows advance planning; union minutes show the plant was occupied; the Pinkerton agents were armed and so were the workers, and both facts appear in testimony.
E

The difference shows up in sequence and in naming. One account begins with the occupation of the plant and the other with the decision to break the union, and where one writes guards the other writes agents.
F
Those choices are not decoration. A reader who accepts the starting point has largely accepted the conclusion, because the first event in a story is the one everything after it is a response to.
G
The practical skill is to notice the first sentence. Ask what happened before it, and whether the author had to choose not to start there.

sequence: the order in which events are told, which can carry an argument without stating one.
connection

title: The Second That Was Added to a Year

p: A
There are two ways to say what time it is. One counts the rotation of the earth. The other counts oscillations of a caesium atom, which is far steadier than the planet.
B

The planet is not a reliable clock. Tides exert a drag that slows the rotation over long periods, and shorter wobbles come from the atmosphere, the oceans and movements of material deep inside the earth.
C
Atomic time does not wobble, so the two slowly separate. Left alone for long enough, clock noon would drift away from the sun being overhead, by a small amount at first and then by a visible one.
D
The fix adopted in 1972 was the leap second. When the gap approaches a limit, an extra second is inserted into the last minute of a day, and that minute officially contains sixty-one seconds.
E

It works, and it causes trouble. Computer systems that assume every minute has sixty seconds have failed at the insertion, and a leap second cannot be scheduled far ahead because the earth's wobbles are not predictable.
F
In 2022 the international body responsible voted to stop inserting them by 2035, letting the gap grow and dealing with it in a larger correction much later.
G

The decision is a trade. Timekeeping that follows the sky is being loosened in favour of timekeeping that computers can rely on, and a thing that has been true for all of history, that noon means the sun is overhead, becomes approximately true instead.

Paragraph E (i.e. the trouble leap seconds cause) and paragraph G (i.e. what the 2035 decision trades away).
summarize
Summarize the leap second and why it is being abandoned.

Earth's rotation is slowed by tides and wobbled by the atmosphere and oceans, so it drifts from atomic time. Since 1972 a leap second has been inserted to keep clock noon near the sun overhead, but computers assuming sixty-second minutes have failed and the insertions cannot be scheduled far ahead, so the practice is to stop by 2035.
vocabulary

oscillation: one complete back-and-forth cycle, counted in an atom to define a second.
leap second: an extra second inserted into the last minute of a day to keep clock time near the earth's rotation.
connection
Describe the connection between the earth's wobbles and the scheduling of leap seconds.

title: The Ship That Was Built Too Tall

p: A
The warship Vasa sailed from Stockholm on its first voyage in August 1628. It travelled roughly 1,300 metres, heeled over in a gust, took water through its open gunports and sank in the harbour.
B
The ship was extraordinarily ornamented and carried two full decks of guns. It was also narrow for its height, and it had far too little ballast in the hold to balance the weight above the waterline.
C

The problem was known before it sailed. An officer had thirty men run from side to side across the deck while the ship lay at the quay, and the rolling became dangerous enough that he stopped the test.
D
The test was not reported upward in any way that stopped the launch. The king had ordered the ship, the king was at war, and the people who knew were not the people who decided.
E

Shipbuilding then had no written calculation of stability. A master shipwright worked from proportions carried in his head and from ships that had worked before, and this ship had been altered during construction.
F
The inquiry afterwards found nobody at fault. The shipwright had died, the surviving builders said they had followed instruction, and the instruction had come from a king nobody was going to name.
G

Vasa was raised almost intact in 1961, because the Baltic is too brackish for the shipworm that would have eaten it anywhere else. The failure is in a museum, which is a rare thing for a failure to be.

Summarize why Vasa sank and why nobody was held responsible.

title: The Forest That Is One Tree

p: A
In central Utah there is a stand of quaking aspen covering about forty-three hectares. It looks like a forest of perhaps forty thousand separate trees, and it is one organism.
B
Aspen reproduce mainly by sending up new stems from a spreading root system. Each stem is genetically identical to the others, and the whole connected mass is called a clone.
C

Testing that is not a matter of looking. Genetic sampling across the stand returns the same profile, the stems are male throughout, and they leaf out and turn colour together in a way neighbouring stands do not.
D

The organism has been given a name, Pando, and an age, and the age is the contested part. Estimates have ranged from several thousand to tens of thousands of years, and the methods behind them disagree.
E
The difficulty is that no individual stem is old. A stem lives perhaps a hundred and fifty years, so the age being claimed belongs to the root system, and a root system does not keep rings.
F
The clone is also in trouble. Surveys find plenty of mature stems and very few young ones, which is what a population looks like when something is eating the new growth faster than it appears.
G
Fenced areas within the stand have begun to regenerate, which points at browsing by deer and elk. It is an unusual conservation problem: the patient is not dying, it is failing to replace itself.

title: The Parts That Had to Fit

p: A

A craftsman building a musket fitted every part to the gun in front of him. A lock from one weapon would not fit another, and a broken part was repaired by a person with files rather than replaced from a box.
B

Making parts interchangeable sounds like a small change and is not. It requires that two parts made months apart in different places fall within a tolerance, which means the tolerance has to be written down and measurable.
C
So the real invention was not a machine. It was a system of gauges, a go gauge that a correct part passes and a no-go gauge it must not pass, together with the discipline of using them on every part.
D

Eli Whitney is often credited, on the strength of a demonstration in Washington in 1801 in which he assembled locks from mixed parts. Later examination of his surviving muskets suggests the parts were not in fact interchangeable.
E
What actually produced the system was slower and less quotable. Armouries in Massachusetts and Virginia worked at it for decades, and interchangeability arrived in the 1840s at considerable expense.
F
The consequence reached far past weapons. Interchangeable parts made repair possible without a craftsman, made assembly a sequence of simple steps, and made the production line thinkable.
G
The story is usually told as a flash of genius because that shape is easier to remember. The accurate version is about measurement, record-keeping and forty years of institutional patience.

title: What the Permafrost Holds

p: A

Permafrost is ground that has stayed below freezing for at least two consecutive years, and in parts of Siberia, Alaska and Canada it runs hundreds of metres deep and has been frozen for a very long time.
B
Frozen ground does not rot. Plants and animals that died there were buried and held rather than broken down, so the permafrost contains an enormous quantity of carbon that never completed its decay.
C

Estimates put that store at well over a thousand billion tonnes, which is roughly twice the carbon currently in the atmosphere. The figure is uncertain, because measuring it means drilling across a region the size of a continent.
D

Thawing releases it, and the form matters. Decay with oxygen produces carbon dioxide; decay in waterlogged ground without oxygen produces methane, which traps far more heat per molecule over the following decades.
E

The worry is that this is a feedback. Warming thaws ground, thawed ground releases gas, and the released gas contributes to further warming, which is a loop that does not require anyone to do anything more to continue.
F
The size and speed of that loop are genuinely unsettled. Thaw is patchy, some ground collapses abruptly while some warms slowly, and plants growing on thawed land take up carbon of their own.
G
So the honest statement has a wide range in it. The store is real and large, the mechanism is understood, and how much arrives this century is a number nobody can yet give with confidence.
